newsitem.title: UK: Violence erupts ahead of N.Ireland march.
newsitem.headline: Violence erupts ahead of N.Ireland march.

text.p: Northern Ireland police moved into Portadown's Garvaghy Road Catholic enclave on Sunday, taking control of the route of a disputed parade by the Protestant Orange Order. Residents attacked them with rocks and petrol bombs.

Witnesses said about 100 police in riot gear arrived on the Garvaghy Road a few hours before dawn and took up positions close to the march route through the mainly Protestant town's Roman Catholic residential district.
Hundreds of residents emerged from their houses and hurled a barrage of rocks and petrol bombs at police, who arrived in armoured jeeps, the witnesses said.
Several residents were injured by plastic bullets fired by police. "This is brute force," a middle-aged woman screamed at the police.
Catholic residents want Sunday's parade banned. No decision had been announced by police or the British government.
Residents said they believed the police action meant the security forces would try to force either the full parade or a token march down the road in coming hours.
The parade has become an annual set piece struggle symbolising the conflict between Protestant and Catholic communities.
Several hundred local Orangemen planned to set out at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT) from the centre of town with banners and bands and, after a service at Drumcree Anglican church, return along Garvaghy Road.

Dozens more Protestant parades are to be staged this week in the build-up to the 12th of July, the most cherished date in the Orange calendar which marks a 17th century Protestant victory over Britain's last Catholic king.

Garvaghy road residents had camped out on the pavements under Irish tricolour flags to claim the area as their own while the town's mainly Protestant people gathered under British Union Jack flags to speculate what the authorities would announce.

The Orange Order, named after the Protestant monarch William of Orange, says their ancestors have staged similar celebrations of their religion and British allegiance for decades and should not be prevented from what they intend as a peaceful demonstration.

Last year police did ban the parade but after almost five days of Protestant rioting they reversed their decision and hurried it through Garvaghy Road, igniting a wave of Catholic fury instead which blazed for several more days.

This year's planned march has confronted Britain's new Labour government with its first major political test of pledges to give equal rights to the pro-British Protestant majority and pro-Irish Catholic minority.

It has also clouded the backdrop to Anglo-Irish attempts to breathe new life into a Northern Ireland peace process which has been brought to its knees by guerrilla violence and mistrust by political leaders of both communities.
Britain has offered Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), a place at peace talks if the IRA calls an end to its war against British rule of the province.
But officials of the two governments say they do not expect the IRA to show its hand until the so-called marching season is over.
Sinn Fein has challenged Britain to prove its commitment to respecting civil rights by stopping the Portadown parade.
